# Summary {#part-frontiers-summary .unnumbered}

The frontiers part took up the three limits that compute does not lift. Learning runs on a finite stock of human text, and every escape route changes the shape of that problem rather than removing it: synthetic data, reward from a checkable environment, more compute at inference, models that keep learning after deployment. For measurement, a task-length horizon reports progress that a saturated benchmark hides, but the quoted horizon is a fifty-percent-reliability number, and in the original fits the horizon at the reliability a deployment needs was several times shorter. For verification, the part's working hypothesis is that in many domains generating a claim is cheap and checking it is not.

Across the three chapters, the binding constraint has moved from production to acceptance. A frontier system can produce candidate answers, programs, proofs, designs, and hypotheses faster than institutions in many fields can confirm them. What is scarce is the evidence and institutional basis that make a result acceptable, and that basis is built from proof objects, replications, adversarial review, and the operating record of whoever vouches for the work.

The open question is whether proof, replication, oversight, and the operating contracts that Part XII develops for deployed systems can scale quickly enough to keep accepted knowledge from becoming the bottleneck. The question is also economic, since who pays for verification and whose verification counts are settled in a market rather than a lab. Part XI turns to ecosystem and economics, where the cost of capability, the terms under which it is released, and the structure of the industry selling it become part of the architecture.
